Given counts x₁ and x₂ observed over time intervals T₁ and T₂, the posterior distributions for their respective rates r₁ and r₂ are Gamma-distributed. The ratio ρ = r₁/r₂ then follows a Beta-prime distribution when flat priors are assumed. This is derived by transforming the joint posterior of (r₁, r₂) into the ratio variable ρ. The key insight is that this transformation preserves analytical tractability, allowing for exact computation of moments and credible intervals. The prior elicitation trick sets α₀ slightly above 1 to ensure r = 0 is excluded, which avoids pathological behavior in zero-count cases. The dual nature of the problem—predictive inference (Skellam) versus inferential (ratio-of-rates)—is resolved by recognizing that the latter provides a more direct measure of relative performance. Failure modes include singularities at x₂ = 0 and sensitivity to prior parametrization, especially in Model A vs Model B formulations. These issues are mitigated through careful choice of priors and explicit modeling of rate differences rather than raw counts.
